title: Unique Paths
summary: Given the dimensions m and n of an m x n grid, where the robot starts at the top-left corner (grid[0][0]) and aims to reach the bottom-right corner (grid[m - 1][n - 1]), with the robot able to move only right or down at any point, return the total number of unique paths the robot can take to reach the destination.
statement: Given the dimensions m and n of an m x n grid, where the robot starts at the top-left corner (grid[0][0]) and aims to reach the bottom-right corner (grid[m - 1][n - 1]), with the robot able to move only right or down at any point, return the total number of unique paths the robot can take to reach the destination. The test cases are structured such that the solution will not exceed 2 * 10^9.
constraints: 1 <= m,n <= 100. The answer is at most 2×10^9.
Start at the top-left cell, finish at the bottom-right cell, and move only right or down.
hints: Every route into a cell comes from above or from its left.
Store path counts for one row and update them left to right.
Initialize a row of ones; on each later row set ways[c] += ways[c-1] for c>0.
A one-row or one-column grid has exactly one route, and a 1×1 grid needs no moves.
editorial: All cells in the first row have one route because only right moves are possible. For each subsequent row, add the count from the previous column in the current row to the old count from the same column in the previous row. The final entry counts all routes to the destination. The oracle uses a binomial coefficient rather than this recurrence.

tests.explanation: Each route contains two down moves and six right moves. Choosing the two down positions among eight gives 28 routes.
The possible move orders are DDR, DRD, and RDD, so there are three routes.
